definition: The empirical rule that the frequency of a word is roughly inversely proportional to its rank in the corpus.
details: In natural language the most common word appears about twice as often as the second most common, three times as often as the third, and so on. Zipfian (power-law) structure appears throughout text and explains why tokenizers work well and why long-tail words are rare — an important fact when modeling language.
story: Picture a translator at the United Nations, listening to one language and whispering the meaning into another in real time. Here is the short version: The empirical rule that the frequency of a word is roughly inversely proportional to its rank in the corpus. The part that makes it sing: In natural language the most common word appears about twice as often as the second most common, three times as often as the third, and so on. Meaning lives in company — a word is known by the words it keeps. And that is Zipf's Law — teaching a machine to read between the lines.
